newsitem.title: USA: Marriott to buy Renaissance for $1 billion, outbids Doubletree.
newsitem.headline: Marriott to buy Renaissance for $1 billion, outbids Doubletree.

text.p: Marriott International Inc. said Tuesday it agreed to acquire Renaissance Hotel Group NV for $1 billion in a cash deal that beat out an earlier bid from Doubletree Corp. of $850 million.
At the same time, Doubletree announced that it was calling off its acquisition of Renaissance, saying it did not want to start a bidding war for the Netherlands-based company.
Following the news, the stock of Renaissance jumped $4.50 to $29.625 on the New York Stock Exchange, and Doubletree gained $2.375 to $43 on Nasdaq. Marriott added 87.5 cents to $56.125 on the NYSE.

Marriott said its $1 billion bid, which would soak up Renaissance's debt, was worth $30 a share. It said 54 percent of the holders of Renaissance's voting stock agreed to the deal and said it will launch a tender for the balance of the shares within five days.
Renaissance operates and franchises 150 hotels in 38 countries. Its brands include New World and Ramada.

Marriott, which is based in Washington, said it operates about 4,700 units in the United States and 29 other countries under the Marriott, Ritz-Carlton, Courtyard, Fairfield, Residence Inn, TownePlace Suites and Marriott Executive Residences brands.
Combined, the companies would have more than 1,300 hotels worldwide across 10 brands, Marriott said. It said it anticipates annual cost savings of $15 million to $20 million from the merger.
"This acquisition provides a dramatic increase in rooms and market position for Marriott International," said J.W. Marriott, Jr., chairman and chief executive officer of Marriott International.

"With the addition of these three outstanding brands to our portfolio, we immediately will reach customers in 40 new markets including Russia, China, Japan, India, Italy and Turkey, and more than double our presence outside of the United States," he said.
Doubletree said its board decided not to pursue its acquisition of Renaissance in light of the agreement between Renaissance and Marriott.
In December, Phoenix, Ariz.-based Doubletree proposed to acquire Renaissance in a stock and cash transaction valued at $850 million, including assumption of $70 million in debt.
"After completing our due diligence, we continue to believe the offer we made for Renaissance is full and fair," said Richard Kelleher, president and chief executive officer of Doubletree.

"Meeting or exceeding the offer that has been made for Renaissance by Marriott International would result in dilution to Doubletree's earnings per share in the next few years, which is not an acceptable option for us," he said.
Doubletree said that under the terms of the Jan. 5 memorandum of understanding between it and Renaissance, Doubletree will receive a break-up fee of $15 million.
